title: Detecting Hidden Nonlinear High Frequency Modes Beyond Fundamental Minimal Temporal Resolution Using Weak Measurements
abstract: In this work we study whether nonlinear models of quantum mechanics can avoid detection by strong measurements, if the nonlinear effects only exist as high frequency modes. A potential physical process which could hide such modes would be amplitude level time averaging over fundamentally indistinguishable times. To that end, we have defined a temporal indistinguishability postulate which describes the averaging process, and handcrafted a nonlinear toy model well suited to avoid detection. We have demonstrated that even in such an ideal setup, tabletop weak postselected measurements can still detect nonlinear behavior and put constraints on nonlinear high frequency modes of evolution, even at frequencies beyond fundamental minimal temporal resolution.
summary: This paper explores the possibility of detecting hidden nonlinearities in quantum mechanics that are masked by fundamental time averaging. By employing weak postselected measurements and a specific toy model, the authors demonstrate that these high-frequency modes leave a detectable signature—a sharp sign flip—in the time-averaged weak value.
main_problem: The work investigates whether nonlinear modifications of quantum mechanics, particularly those manifesting only as high-frequency modes beyond a fundamental temporal resolution ($	au$), can evade detection by standard strong measurements.
main_result: Even when designed to hide nonlinearity from strong time averaging, weak postselected measurements can still detect these hidden high-frequency modes via a characteristic discontinuous sign flip in the time-averaged weak value.
method: The analysis employs weak postselected measurements and applies a 'temporal indistinguishability postulate' (TIP) which mandates amplitude averaging over fundamental time intervals ($	au$).
model_or_system: A handcrafted nonlinear toy model is used, involving a two-level system whose evolution Hamiltonian ($H_q$) contains high-frequency components ($H_{hf}$). The nonlinearity is designed to be invisible under standard strong measurements.
key_observables: The time-averaged weak value $(\sigma_z)_w$ of the $\sigma_z$ observable, which exhibits a discontinuous sign flip at specific parameter ratios.
important_parameters: Three crucial scales are compared: experimental clock resolution ($\Delta t_{\exp}$), fundamental indistinguishability scale ($	au$), and the high-frequency mode period ($\Omega^{-1}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a fundamental time scale $	au$ (TIP) and relies on using a specific, handcrafted nonlinear toy model.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the problem concerning nonlinearity evasion, then introducing the TIP and the weak measurement framework. The core is the calculation of the time-averaged weak value via contour integration, leading to the identification of the sign-flipping transition condition that signals hidden nonlinearities.
why_interesting: This work provides a theoretical mechanism showing how non-standard quantum effects (high-frequency nonlinearity) might be probed using advanced measurement techniques (weak measurements) even when standard methods fail due to averaging assumptions.
